profile.reading:
This building sits at 18844 FM 1957 near Castroville, Texas, about 27 miles west of downtown San Antonio, on a rural Medina County site that trade publication CoStar has identified as home to Microsoft's SAT80, SAT81, and SAT82 data center buildings together. CoStar's 2024 report on a newer $482.6 million SAT82 building at the same address described SAT80 and SAT81 as standing there under an earlier, separate investment of more than $230 million, a figure that matches a Medina County Microsoft project the San Antonio Current separately reported without naming a specific SAT code. CoStar characterized all three buildings as colocation data centers built to rent capacity to third party tenant companies rather than exclusively hosting Microsoft's own cloud workloads, a characterization this registry repeats as CoStar's own framing rather than something Microsoft itself has confirmed publicly.

The San Antonio Report has separately described what it called the SAT80-1 and SAT80-2 buildings at this same rural site as each exceeding 106,000 square feet on a shared 206 acre parcel. That reporting predates CoStar's later account of the SAT82 expansion, so this registry cannot confirm whether the San Antonio Report's SAT80-1 and SAT80-2 labels map directly onto this building and its SAT80 neighbor, or whether they describe an earlier two building phase that this registry's own SAT80 and SAT81 records correspond to only loosely. Microsoft has built at least eight data centers across the San Antonio region, spanning Bexar and Medina counties, since first opening two facilities there in 2015 at roughly $90 million each, with cumulative regional investment exceeding $1.2 billion as of August 2023. San Antonio's city council approved a 15 year Chapter 380 tax reimbursement in 2013 covering 40 percent of property taxes in exchange for a $250 million Microsoft investment commitment and 20 new jobs, and Microsoft's continued expansion into rural Medina County reflects the same pattern of steadily broadening its footprint well beyond that original commitment.

CPS Energy, San Antonio's municipally owned electric and gas utility, supplies power to this site and has cited large commercial and industrial customers, data centers among them, in its own integrated resource planning as it weighs new generation for growing demand. Because CPS Energy is municipally owned rather than investor owned, large load agreements with customers like Microsoft are negotiated directly with the city owned utility rather than through the Public Utility Commission of Texas process governing most of the state's investor owned utilities. No total campus megawatt figure for this site was found in sourcing reviewed this session.

reading.body:
SAT81 sits on a shared 206-acre rural campus in Medina County, Texas, about 27 miles west of downtown San Antonio, alongside two other Microsoft data center buildings (SAT80 and SAT82) totaling roughly 456,000 square feet across three structures. The three buildings together occupy a single site but their individual power consumption has not been published by Microsoft or found in available reporting. At standard AI training density of roughly 40 kilowatts per rack, a 100 megawatt campus would hold approximately 2,500 racks, though the actual power draw of this specific facility and how it divides among the three buildings remain unknown.

The Medina County campus received initial investment exceeding $230 million for what trade sources identify as colocation-capable data centers, followed by a $482.6 million expansion (SAT82, completed early 2028) on the same parcel. Power at the site flows through CPS Energy, San Antonio's municipally owned utility, under a negotiated large load agreement rather than through the Public Utility Commission of Texas regulatory process that covers investor-owned utilities elsewhere in the state. Microsoft's cumulative investment across at least eight facilities in the San Antonio region exceeded $1.2 billion as of August 2023, supported by a 15-year property tax reimbursement the city approved in 2013.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities, of which 19 have published power specifications totaling 475 megawatts; this campus ranks outside the top 19 in published capacity and therefore contributes an unknown figure to the state's total. Because the individual megawatt capacity of SAT81 and its two co-located buildings has never been disclosed, this facility cannot be ranked or assessed against other AI compute hubs by power draw, making its actual significance to regional or national AI scaling unclear from public sources.
